pedagogy.summary:
• Age/Topic: Ages 7–9 — coral reefs are built by tiny living animals called coral polyps (reefs are not rock), reefs host more species than almost any other ocean habitat, and are called the 'rainforests of the sea'.
• Standards — UK (DfE Lower KS2): Y4 'recognise that environments can change and that this can sometimes pose dangers to living things' and habitats/food-chain strands — the reef as a super-rich habitat and later a threatened one.
• Standards — US (NGSS): 3-LS4-3/3-LS4-4 (habitats and environmental change) and 2-LS4-1/biodiversity framing — the reef as the ocean's biodiversity hotspot.
• Operational details: three ideas — (1) coral is a colony of tiny living ANIMALS (polyps), not a plant and not rock; the hard reef is the limestone they build; (2) reefs are astonishingly biodiverse — a small area holds a huge variety of life; (3) the 'rainforests of the sea' analogy captures both the biodiversity and the reef-as-structure-that-shelters-others. The polyp-is-an-animal fact is the key surprise; the biodiversity is the wonder. (Bleaching/threats are the KS3 dependent — keep light here.)
• Checkpoint — Tier A (~7–8): states coral is made by tiny living animals, not rock; Tier B (~8–9): describes a reef as one of the most life-packed habitats; Tier C (~9): explains the rainforest analogy (huge biodiversity + a structure that houses countless other species).
bestPractices: Lead with the counter-intuitive core fact — coral is a living ANIMAL (a polyp), not a plant or a rock — using close-up footage of polyps feeding to make it vivid and believable.
Zoom across scales: single polyp → colony → whole reef, so children see how tiny builders make a giant structure over long time.
Make biodiversity concrete with a 'how many species can you spot?' count in one reef patch, then compare to a barer seabed — richness is felt by contrast.
Unpack the rainforest analogy explicitly on two grounds: (a) exceptional variety of life, (b) the reef, like a forest, is a physical structure that provides homes/food for everything else.
Connect to prior habitat and food-web learning — the reef is a habitat and the base structure of a dense web.
keyRepresentations: A zoom sequence: coral polyp → coral colony → whole reef
A close-up of a polyp (tentacles, mouth) labelled 'a tiny living animal'
A biodiversity 'spot-the-species' reef scene vs a bare seabed for contrast
A side-by-side reef ↔ rainforest analogy panel (variety + structure that shelters others)
commonMisconceptions: 'Coral is a rock / a stone' — not knowing the reef is built by living animals (only the limestone skeleton is hard).
'Coral is a plant' — misled by its branching, flower-like, rooted appearance.
'A reef is one big creature' — rather than a colony of many tiny polyps (and a whole community).
'Reefs are colourful decorations' — missing that they are the most biodiverse marine habitat and shelter for countless species.
Taking 'rainforests of the sea' as being about greenery/plants rather than about biodiversity and structure.

learn.summary: For ages 7–9: coral reefs are built by colonies of tiny living ANIMALS called polyps (the hard reef is the limestone skeleton they build — made by living animals, not just lifeless rock, and not a plant); reefs are among the most biodiverse marine habitats; and they are called 'rainforests of the sea' because of both their variety of life and their role as a living structure that shelters countless other species. The counter-intuitive 'coral is alive — it's an animal' fact is the key surprise; the biodiversity is the wonder. Keep bleaching/threats light at this stage.

activities.title: Zoom from reef to a single living polyp
feedback: If a learner says the reef 'isn't alive' or is 'just rock the fish live on', show or describe a close-up of a polyp's tentacles feeding and name the animal vs its limestone house — like a snail is alive but its shell is hard.

If a learner says coral 'makes its own food from sunlight like a plant' or calls it seaweed, clarify: tiny algae living inside the coral use sunlight, but the coral itself is an animal that also catches prey — a partnership, not a plant. Contrast with true seaweed. (Bring this detail in only when the plant idea is raised; the core message stays 'coral is an animal'.)
If a learner thinks a reef is one big creature, remind them it is a colony of many tiny polyps forming a whole community.
activities.rationale: Leading with the close-up of a feeding polyp and a scale reveal from reef to single animal targets the dominant misconceptions (coral is a rock / a plant / one big creature) directly, letting children see an animal behaviour that a rock never shows.
sourceClaims: Coral reefs are built by colonies of tiny living animals called coral polyps, which secrete a hard calcium-carbonate skeleton; coral is an animal, not a plant or rock.
learnerActions: Start with a view of a whole busy reef, then step inward: reef → one branch of coral → a single polyp with its ring of tentacles and a mouth.
Name what you see at the smallest scale: a tiny living animal, not a rock or a stone.
State in your own words how billions of these tiny animals, each building a hard limestone cup around itself, add up to the giant reef structure over long time.
Explain what tells you a polyp is an animal and not a plant (it has a mouth and catches drifting food with stinging tentacles; seaweed has no mouth or tentacles and makes its food from sunlight).
activities.intendedInsight: The hard reef is the limestone skeleton that colonies of tiny living animals (polyps) build; coral is an animal, not a rock or a plant.

activities.title: Count the species: reef versus bare seabed
feedback: If the learner undercounts, prompt them to look for hidden and small animals (in crevices, on the coral surface), not just the large fish.
Reinforce that the point is the number of DIFFERENT kinds of living things, not just how many animals total.
activities.rationale: Richness is abstract until felt by contrast; a hands-on spot-and-tally against a sparse seabed makes biodiversity concrete for this age.
sourceClaims: Coral reefs are among the most biodiverse ecosystems on Earth — occupying a tiny fraction of the ocean yet supporting about a quarter of all marine species — which is why they are called 'rainforests of the sea'.
learnerActions: Explore one reef scene and tap or point to each different creature; keep a running tally of how many distinct species you can spot.
Do the same count on a bare patch of seabed and compare the two tallies.
Say in a sentence what the contrast shows about how much variety of life a small reef area holds.
activities.intendedInsight: Reefs are among the most biodiverse habitats in the ocean — a tiny area holds a huge variety of life, felt most strongly by contrast with a barer habitat.

activities.title: Unpack the 'rainforests of the sea' analogy
feedback: If a learner explains the nickname by bright colours or plants, reframe to the huge number of different living things sheltered, and to the reef-as-structure idea — point back to the species tally and the living build from the zoom activity.
Encourage connecting to earlier habitat and food-web learning: the reef is both a habitat and the base structure of a dense web of life.
activities.rationale: Explicitly separating the two grounds of the analogy prevents the common misreading of the phrase as being about greenery, and ties biodiversity to structure.
sourceClaims: Coral reefs are among the most biodiverse ecosystems on Earth — occupying a tiny fraction of the ocean yet supporting about a quarter of all marine species — which is why they are called 'rainforests of the sea'.
learnerActions: Look at a side-by-side comparison of a reef and a rainforest.
List two reasons the names match: (a) exceptional variety of life, and (b) both are physical living structures that provide homes and food for everything else.
Explain why the nickname is NOT mainly about colour or greenery/plants.
activities.intendedInsight: The analogy captures biodiversity AND the reef as a living structure that shelters other species — like a forest provides homes for forest animals.

activities.title: Grow a reef over time (optional dynamic model)
feedback: If the learner thinks the reef appeared all at once, highlight the time-lapse: reefs build up slowly from countless tiny animals.
Connect the climbing species counter back to the reef-versus-bare-seabed comparison, noting that more varied structure tends to support more kinds of life.
activities.rationale: A time-lapse builder adds time and the tiny-builders-make-a-giant-structure sequence that a static scene cannot show, though the core facts do not require it.
sourceClaims: Coral reefs are built by colonies of tiny living animals called coral polyps, which secrete a hard calcium-carbonate skeleton; coral is an animal, not a plant or rock.
learnerActions: Seed a few polyps and watch (or step through) as they divide and secrete limestone, building structure over time.
Watch a species counter climb as the growing structure attracts more animals.
Say how this shows that tiny builders make a giant structure, and that a larger, more complex structure tends to provide homes for more kinds of animals.
activities.intendedInsight: Tiny living builders make a giant structure over long time; in this model a larger, more complex structure tends to offer more homes, so biodiversity tends to increase as the reef grows.

activities.title: Check your understanding
feedback: For a 'rock' or 'plant' answer, return to the polyp close-up and the animal-feeding evidence.
For an analogy answer based on colour, redirect to variety of life and structure-that-shelters-others.
activities.rationale: Short justify-your-answer questions can confirm coverage of the three evidence goals as a companion check; recognition questions confirm knowledge but do not by themselves elicit the fuller explanation produced in the construction activities, so justification is required here.
learnerActions: Answer: is coral a rock, a plant, or an animal? Justify your choice.
Compare the variety of life on a reef with that on a bare seabed and say which is more biodiverse.
Explain in a sentence why reefs are called the 'rainforests of the sea'.
activities.intendedInsight: Learners can state and justify all three core ideas: polyp-is-an-animal, reef biodiversity, and the analogy.

activities.title: Meet a talking coral polyp (optional spark)
feedback: Use the polyp's answers to reinforce: the animal is the polyp, the hard part is the house it builds.
If the role-play drifts, bring it back to the three core facts with the close-up and the species tally.
activities.rationale: A character voice can spark wonder and motivate questions; the three core facts and the scale reveal are presented in the visual activities, so this dialogue is offered as a complement rather than the main carrier of those facts.
learnerActions: Interview a polyp character (or a reef biologist) who explains in role: 'I'm an animal!', how its colony built the reef over a long time, and how it catches food while staying fixed in one place, using its moving tentacles.
Ask your own wonder questions and compare the answers to what you learned from the zoom and counting activities.
activities.intendedInsight: A polyp's first-person account can make the 'it's alive and it's an animal' surprise memorable and invite curiosity.

constraints: Keep bleaching and reef threats light at this stage; the detailed threat/cause reasoning is a later (KS3) dependent.

The 'coral has algae living inside it that use sunlight' detail appears in the assessment answer and explains why reefs grow in shallow sunlit water; it is advanced for the 7–9 state-the-facts goal — introduce only as an extension, and only when a learner raises the plant/sunlight idea, and do not let it replace the core 'coral is an animal' message.

Recognition questions (is it a rock/plant/animal?) confirm knowledge but do not by themselves elicit the independent explanation; pair them with activities where the child states and justifies the ideas.

Optional interaction examples (tap-to-name, zoom drill-down, reef↔seabed toggle, species counter, linked analogy panel, time-lapse builder, character dialogue) make the mechanism concrete but are not mandatory; the learning can be delivered with pictures, counting on paper, or discussion.
The 3D swim-through and the dynamic builder are enrichment; the learning goals do not hinge on spatial navigation or on time-lapse mechanics.
The structure→biodiversity link in the optional builder is a general ecological idea, not a figure established by the cited sources; keep it qualified ('tends to') and model-descriptive.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of a saved teaching-research row without fresh source verification; the two NOAA sources were marked verified:false in the original and have NOT been re-fetched. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

The source assessment states reef-building corals 'house tiny algae inside their body that make food from sunlight'. This is biologically accurate (zooxanthellae) but is a notable step beyond the stated 7–9 evidence goals; verify age-appropriateness before foregrounding it.
The claim that reefs support 'about a quarter of all marine species' comes from the cited NOAA source and has not been independently re-verified here.

The 'more structure brings more biodiversity' relationship in the optional 'grow a reef' model is a general ecological generalisation and is not directly asserted by either cited source; it is kept qualified and presented as what the model shows.

The original framed the interactive image as the uniquely ideal medium and other media as lesser; this rewrite preserves the alternatives as genuinely useful without asserting comparative efficacy, which the sources do not establish.

probeDeeper: You said it's alive — what would we expect to see a living coral DO that a rock never does?
Reefs only build up in shallow, clear, sunny water. Why would an animal 'need' sunlight — unless something living inside it does?
If the water got so cloudy that no sunlight reached the coral, what do you predict would happen to it, and why?
A sea anemone in a rock pool and a coral polyp are close cousins. What is the one big difference between them?
assess.correctAnswer: A coral is a living thing — the hard reef is made by huge colonies of tiny animals called polyps, each like a minute sea anemone in a little cup of limestone it builds around itself. It doesn't chase food: it catches tiny drifting plankton with stinging tentacles, and (in reef-building corals) it also houses tiny algae inside its body that make food from sunlight, which is why reefs grow in shallow, sunlit, warm water. The rock is what the animals build, not the animal itself.

errorPatterns.pattern: 'Coral is a rock / a stone you find in the sea' — treats the hard reef as non-living because it is hard and doesn't move.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Show a close-up video of extended polyp tentacles feeding at night; name the polyp as the animal and the limestone as its skeleton/house — the same way a snail is alive but its shell is hard.
errorPatterns.distractor: It's a colourful rock on the seabed — rocks aren't alive, so coral isn't either.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Says the reef isn't alive, or that it's 'just rock that fish live on'; surprised that anything animal-like is involved.

errorPatterns.pattern: 'Coral is a plant / seaweed' — because it is fixed in place, branching and colourful, so it must be like a plant growing up from the bottom.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Distinguish: the ALGAE living inside the coral do use sunlight, but the coral itself is an animal that also catches prey — a partnership, not a plant. Contrast with true seaweed nearby.
errorPatterns.distractor: It's a plant — it's fixed down and branches like one, so it grows from the seabed like seaweed.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Says coral 'makes its own food from sunlight like a plant' with no mention of the animal, or calls it a kind of seaweed.

errorPatterns.pattern: '"Rainforest of the sea" means it is pretty/full of plants' — reads the phrase as about colour or vegetation rather than biodiversity.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Reframe: like a rainforest, a reef packs an enormous VARIETY of species into a small space; count the different animals visible in one photo.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Explains the nickname by the bright colours, not by the huge number of different living things it shelters.

responseLevels.gap: Calls coral a rock or a plant; denies it is an animal, or cannot say how a fixed thing could feed.
responseLevels.full: Explains that the reef is built by colonies of tiny animal polyps that both catch plankton and host sunlight-using algae, and uses that to explain why reefs grow in warm shallow sunlit seas and why 'rainforest of the sea' means biodiversity — transferring the idea to predict what harms a reef.
responseLevels.partial: Knows coral is a living animal and that reefs are rich in life, but treats these as separate facts — can't connect the polyp's feeding (plankton + algae partners) to why reefs need shallow sunlit water.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Here is a photo of a coral reef, all knobbly and colourful. I tell you a coral reef is alive — it is built by thousands of tiny animals. Is that true, and if a coral is an animal, how does it eat and grow when it never moves around like a fish does?
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: A child who thinks coral is a rock or a plant will say it isn't really alive, or that it 'grows like a plant from the seabed', and cannot explain feeding by an animal that stays put. A child with the concept separates the living polyp from the limestone it secretes and gives a plausible non-chasing way to eat (catching plankton / algae partners). Asking HOW a fixed animal eats is the discriminator — a rock/plant view has no answer to it.
